title: Law of Demeter & Tell, Don't Ask
summary: Talk only to your immediate collaborators, and tell an object what to do instead of pulling its data out to decide elsewhere.

slides.markdown:
The **Law of Demeter** says: only call methods on objects you directly hold — your parameters, your fields, objects you create — not on objects you reached to get from one of those. **Tell, Don't Ask** is the companion habit: push behavior to the object that owns the data, instead of pulling the data out to decide with it elsewhere.

Both are coupling principles SOLID doesn't explicitly name: "don't talk to strangers." A method chain like `a.getB().getC().doSomething()` is the visible symptom this topic teaches you to spot and fix.

slides.sectionTitle: The Law of Demeter: "don't talk to strangers"
slides.markdown:
The Law of Demeter restricts which objects a method is allowed to call methods on: its own fields, its parameters, objects it creates itself, and objects returned by any of those — but not objects obtained by chaining further through *those* returned objects.

Concretely, if `order.getCustomer()` returns a `Customer`, calling `order.getCustomer().getAddress()` is already reaching one hop too far — `Address` is a "stranger" to whatever method wrote that line, known only through an object it doesn't directly own. The rule isn't about method-chain syntax specifically; it's about how many objects deep your code needs to understand to do its job.

A chain like `order.getCustomer().getAddress().getCountry().getTaxRate()` is nicknamed a **train wreck** — each `.get` is another car coupling the caller to another object's internal structure. The caller now depends on: `Order` having a `Customer`, `Customer` having an `Address`, `Address` having a `Country`, and `Country` having a `getTaxRate()` — four separate things that can each break this one line if any of them changes shape.

The deeper problem isn't the syntax, it's that this code now *knows* the entire path through the object graph just to get one value — knowledge that should have been the responsibility of something closer to the data.

slides.sectionTitle: Tell, Don't Ask: pushing behavior to the object that owns the data
slides.markdown:
**Tell, Don't Ask** is Demeter's sibling principle for behavior instead of navigation: instead of asking an object for its internal data (`account.getBalance()`) and then deciding what to do with it elsewhere (`if (balance < amount) throw ...`), **tell** the object what you want done (`account.withdraw(amount)`) and let it enforce its own rules.

The caller in the "ask" version has to know the withdrawal rule and re-implement it correctly every time it withdraws — miss one call site and you've got an inconsistent, unenforced rule. The "tell" version keeps the rule in exactly one place: inside `Account`, next to the data it protects.

slides.sectionTitle: Code: refactoring a getter chain into a single delegated call
Compare: strict Demeter compliance vs pragmatic exceptions
slides.markdown:
Applying the Law of Demeter literally everywhere produces its own problems, so most teams draw a pragmatic line:

| | Strict Demeter compliance | Common pragmatic exceptions |
|---|---|---|
| Rule | Never chain past your immediate collaborators, ever | Allow chaining on objects designed to be chained through |
| DTOs / value objects | Even `address.getCity()` on a returned address is flagged | Fine — a data-only object with no behavior isn't hiding a "stranger's" logic, it's just structured data |
| Builders | `new Builder().setX().setY().build()` is flagged as chaining | Fine — the builder itself is the object being configured; each call returns `this`, not a different collaborator |
| Fluent APIs (streams, query builders) | `list.stream().filter(...).map(...)` is flagged | Fine — each link returns the same kind of object by design, not a traversal into unrelated internals |

**How to decide:** the risk Demeter protects against is coupling to another object's *internal structure*. If the chain is walking through structural collaborators (Order → Customer → Address), enforce it strictly; if it's a builder or a data-only value object designed for chaining, relax it.

slides.sectionTitle: Pitfall: "fixing" a train wreck by adding a wrapper method for every chain
slides.markdown:
**Wrong belief:** "Every time I see a chain, I should add a one-line delegating wrapper method to the intermediate class, so the chain becomes two shorter calls."

**Why it's wrong:** mechanically wrapping every hop without thinking about ownership just relocates the train wreck one level up and multiplies the API surface — now `Customer` has a `getAddressCountry()`, `Order` has a `getCustomerCountry()`, and every class has grown pass-through methods that exist only to shorten chains, not to express real behavior.

**Correct model:** push the delegation to whichever object should *own* the resulting capability as a real piece of its behavior (`Order.getTaxRate()`, not `Order.getCustomerAddressCountry()`), and stop the moment you're just relaying a name deeper into the object graph.
